plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.2.9
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to evaluate the double integral of (2x - y^2) over the triangular region R enclosed between y = -x + 1, y = x + 1, and y = 3. The figure shows the triangular region R in the xy-plane with vertices at (-2, 3), (0, 1), and (2, 3); the bounding lines y = 3 (top), y = -x + 1 (lower left), and y = x + 1 (lower right) are labeled. The y-axis divides R into two sub-regions: R1 (shaded blue, left half) and R2 (shaded yellow, right half), each with a red vertical strip indicating the direction of inner integration. The figure illustrates the decomposition of R into two type-I sub-regions required when the lower boundary changes expression across the y-axis.

interactionPlan.concept: A triangular region whose lower boundary has two different formulas must be split into two Type-I subregions for vertical slices, but can be integrated as one region by switching to horizontal slices.

y-axis with arrowhead and label y

dynamic integral-limits display for Type II: 1 <= y <= 3 and 1 - y <= x <= y - 1

interactions.label: Lower boundary equations
interactions.teaches: The two Type-I integrals arise because the lower boundary below y = 3 is described by one formula on the left of the y-axis and a different formula on the right

interactions.label: Slice direction
interactions.teaches: Changing the slicing direction changes the limits of integration; horizontal slices cross the whole triangle at once, so the region no longer needs to be split into R1 and R2

demo_steps.title: View the Type-I split
demo_steps.narration: With vertical slices, the lower edge of the region is y = -x + 1 on the left and y = x + 1 on the right. That change of formula at x = 0 forces the region to be written as R1 plus R2.

demo_steps.title: Connect boundaries to limits
demo_steps.narration: Edit either lower-boundary equation and watch the corresponding shaded subregion and its lower limit update. The displayed limits show why the integral becomes two pieces: one for -2 <= x <= 0 and one for 0 <= x <= 2.

demo_steps.title: Switch the order of integration
demo_steps.narration: Horizontal slices run from the left line to the right line across the entire triangle. The same region can now be described without splitting: 1 <= y <= 3 and 1 - y <= x <= y - 1.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A region is split for integration only when the chosen slice direction makes a boundary change formula; choosing the other slice direction can turn two integrals into one.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw a clean xy-plane with the y-axis passing through the bottom vertex of the inverted triangle and the x-axis below it. The triangle has a cyan outline, a horizontal top edge at y = 3, and lower edges meeting at (0, 1). Shade the left half light blue and label it R1; shade the right half pale yellow and label it R2. In Type-I mode, show two red vertical slice markers and the split along the y-axis. In Type-II mode, fade the left/right color distinction into a single region shade and replace the red vertical strips with one blue horizontal strip spanning from the left boundary to the right boundary. Keep the math labels large and close to their corresponding boundary lines, matching the textbook style.
